questions.knowledge_point: Sketching Cartesian Products in the Coordinate Plane
questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=\{-1,2\}\times \{-3,1\}$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

In this case, computing $\{-1,2\}\times \{-3,1\}$ gives the following set:

$$
S=\{(-1,-3),(-1,1),(2,-3),(2,1)\}.
$$

Our visualization of this set is shown in the diagram below.

questions.knowledge_point: Sketching Cartesian Products in the Coordinate Plane
questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=[-1,1]\times \{-1,1\}$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=[-1,1]\times \{-1,1\}
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is either $-1$ or $1.$

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in [-1,1],\,y\in \{-1,1\}\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $-1$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,-1)\,:\,x\in [-1,1]\}
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/3ed05ffc58aad1a6c75e7862c1175f497fb14870e6650cc6c4ce01c3df091d8b.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1$

$$
{S}_{2}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in [-1,1]\}.
$$

This set is represented by the line segment shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/0f57920b2532177b0d64ac3dc95feb6a476bb385112d736d702895862e7de2b2.png)

Our Cartesian product is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
S={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}
$$

Therefore, $S$ can be represented by the two line segments shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/075454dae9ed36967a70537cdf3a3f59931cdd81671ff4059658d2e0df438898.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Sketching Cartesian Products of Special Sets in the Coordinate Plane
questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=N\times Z$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=N\times Z
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a natural number and whose $y$-coordinate is an integer number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in N,\,y\in Z\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any integer number.

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(1,y)\,:\,y\in Z\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/179fdaa3921cb29f2d25ff97bce262fd13fb2ff591c12e97a33953e95967f6fc.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any natural number.

$$
{S}_{2}=\{(2,y)\,:\,y\in Z\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/7399e42988df8a809013393d8873b6a6e5f60b64c0419eadd7bb3c334eb410d6.png)

We can create the subsets ${S}_{3},{S}_{4},{S}_{5},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product $S$ is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $N\times Z$ as the set of points in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/16ff13c793d3c3f57eefee638fbc1ff83569ef6d084d9d053f8585f72c8812d7.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Visualizing Unions of Uncountable Families of Indexed Sets
questions.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[-i,i]\times \{2i\}.$ Which of the following represents ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for at least one}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[-0.5,0.5]\times \{1\}=\{(k,1)\,:\,k\in [-0.5,0.5]\}.
$$

This represents a horizontal line segment from the point $(-0.5,1)$ to the point $(0.5,1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/6c6aafd9ea78868e953340eaab3862491d275972d690e2ceb27c213dadbcaea6.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[-i,i]\times \{2i\}=\{(k,2i)\,:\,k\in [-i,i]\}
$$

is the horizontal line segment from the point $(-i,2i)$ to the point $(i,2i).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/02c8f93a25d7b510d3e238e6d4a974d6ccc2e83f3ac01fe92ce4535fbb4dce48.png)

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following triangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/3b3cefa03d71d99e4b7f3b6852ed36512d2a841a37c558034eac5c4b6870799c.png)

evidence.solution_quote:
As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following triangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/3b3cefa03d71d99e4b7f3b6852ed36512d2a841a37c558034eac5c4b6870799c.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Visualizing Intersections of Uncountable Families of Indexed Sets
questions.problem: Let $I=[0,2]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=\{i\}\times [0,i].$ Which of the following represents ${⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=1,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{1}=\{1\}\times [0,1]=\{(1,k)\,:\,k\in [0,1]\}.
$$

This represents a vertical line segment from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(1,1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/71dd97607df48caf579c2e476520507ede035f65c336064f022cd900b6c120fc.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=\{i\}\times [0,i]=\{(i,k)\,:\,k\in [0,i]\}
$$

is the vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i,i).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/4b87c830620f54e5b3a3bb7923be971b4d9d4abb98cfb3dcdc8387f376a0b452.png)

There are no points that lie in all sets. Therefore, the intersection of the indexed sets is $∅,$ the empty set.

evidence.solution_quote: There are no points that lie in all sets. Therefore, the intersection of the indexed sets is $∅,$ the empty set.
